newsitem.title: CUBA: Castro says way ahead for Cuba is still not easy.
newsitem.headline: Castro says way ahead for Cuba is still not easy.

text.p: President Fidel Castro said on Saturday that while Cuba was recovering from the worst of its economic crisis, citizens should not think the way ahead would be easy.

Paying tribute to neighbourhood groups called the Comittees for the Defence of the Revolution (CDRs), Castro was also adamant that whatever the pressures from the United States, Cuba would not permit the collapse of its communist system.

"The enemy knows that the (Cuban) people would prefer death one thousand times more than going back to the past (before the 1959 revolution)," Castro told a rally in the central city of Sancti Spiritus to mark the 36th anniversary of the forming of the CDRs.
On the country's emergence from an economic crisis caused by the collapse of its old ally the former Soviet Union, Castro said Cuba would continue to recover but that this could take some time.

"We should feel satisfied at how we are recovering, but we must at the same time be on alert against any tendency to think that the way ahead of us will be a bed of roses," added Castro in a speech broadcast on state radio.

Cuban authorities have predicted economic growth of about five percent this year, measured in terms of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), following GDP growth of 2.5 percent last year and a sharp contraction in the years 1989-1993.
Despite modest improvement, living standards for most Cubans remain way below what they were in the 1980s.
The Cuban leader said the island would not be budged by pressure from the United States, including its recent Helms-Burton law that tightens the longstanding embargo against Havana.
"They still want to swallow us up, they still want to annex us ... but the people say no, they won't succeed."

On the role of CDRs -- the largest of Cuba's mass organisations with membership encompassing some 90 percent of the adult population -- Castro said the groups still had important work to do defending the revolution, helping with political education and fighting crime.
Despite the continued high theoretical membership, Cubans widely agree the CDRs have declined as a force in society in recent years.

In the early years of the revolution, the groups were supposed to be a grass-roots defence against people trying to sabotage the system. For some people they acquired an image of being a means of spying on neighbours.

Nowadays many people, especially the young, do not bother going to CDR meetings. But the groups still organise blood donations, gather recyclable waste material, persuade people to vote in elections and run street cleaning sessions.
